passages.title: Creation
passages.summary: God creates the world and gives humans care of its life. God calls creation good.
passages.uncertainty: No verified location is supplied for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 2 places human creation within God's work. Human dignity shapes how we treat others.

contextNote.title: Creation gives people a shared worth
contextNote.text: The chapter gives people worth before it gives them work. Both women and men bear God’s image. No king receives that status alone. The command to rule follows this shared identity. Read dominion beside the blessing of life, not as permission for abuse.

passages.title: Life in the garden
passages.summary: God rests. God places the man in Eden and forms the woman.
passages.uncertainty: No verified location is supplied for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 3 connects the garden with God's commands. Study work, rest, and partnership together.

contextNote.title: Work does not answer every human need
contextNote.text: The garden provides food and meaningful work, yet the man remains alone. That lack interrupts the repeated goodness of creation. Naming animals does not produce a partner who shares his life. The woman's arrival answers a need that possessions and duties cannot meet.

passages.title: The Fall
passages.summary: The man and woman eat the forbidden fruit. They leave the garden.
passages.uncertainty: No verified location is supplied for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 4 expands the garden account. Second Nephi 2 connects the Fall with choice and redemption.

contextNote.title: Blame changes the relationships in the garden
contextNote.text: The man answers a question about his action by naming the woman. He also reminds God who gave her to him. The woman then names the serpent. These replies show damaged trust before the account describes life outside the garden.

passages.title: Cain and Abel
passages.summary: Cain kills Abel. The chapter follows Cain's family and the birth of Seth.
passages.uncertainty: No verified location is supplied for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 5 adds gospel teaching after the Fall. Compare Cain's choices with Adam and Eve's worship.

contextNote.title: Protection becomes a claim to unlimited revenge
contextNote.text: God's protection keeps Cain from becoming another victim of killing. Lamech later uses that protection to boast about greater revenge. His speech changes a limit on violence into a threat. Growing skills and towns therefore do not guarantee growing restraint.

passages.title: Generations to Noah
passages.summary: The family record traces Adam's line to Noah. Enoch walks with God.
passages.uncertainty: No verified location is supplied for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 6–7 expands Enoch's account. Zion means a people united in righteousness and care.

contextNote.title: One life breaks the repeated ending
contextNote.text: The family list repeatedly ends each long life with death. Enoch's departure interrupts that pattern rather than extending his years. Noah's name then introduces hope for relief from hard work. The list carries both continuity and the unresolved burden of the cursed ground.

passages.title: Noah builds the ark
passages.summary: Violence fills the earth. God tells Noah to build an ark.
passages.uncertainty: No verified location is supplied for this chapter.

lds.text: Moses 8 describes Noah's preaching before the flood. Read preparation alongside the call to repent.

contextNote.title: The flood account begins with violence
contextNote.text: The explanation for destruction concerns a world filled with violence. This description reaches beyond one person's hidden wrongdoing. Noah's work preserves creatures threatened by that human disorder. The account joins judgment on violence with costly preparation to keep life.

passages.title: The flood
passages.summary: Noah's household and the animals enter the ark. The flood covers the land.
passages.uncertainty: No verified location is supplied for this chapter.

lds.text: The Church manual reads Noah's deliverance within God's dealings with humanity. Consider faithful action under warning.

contextNote.title: The closed door marks the limit of safety
contextNote.text: Noah follows the instructions, but God closes the ark's door. That detail separates preparation from control over the coming disaster. The repeated lists of creatures emphasize how much life remains at risk. Survival inside the ark stands beside extensive loss outside it.

passages.title: The waters recede
passages.summary: The ark rests in the mountains of Ararat. Noah leaves and builds an altar.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Noah worships after deliverance. Consider how gratitude can follow a period of waiting.

contextNote.title: The promise concerns ordinary seasons
contextNote.text: The ending names farming, weather, day, and night rather than another rescue. These repeated conditions make future life possible. God's promise follows an admission that human wrongdoing continues. The restored world therefore depends on divine patience, not a newly perfect human community.

passages.title: A covenant with Noah
passages.summary: God gives the rainbow as a covenant sign. Noah's sons receive different blessings.
passages.uncertainty: No verified location is supplied for this chapter.

lds.text: A covenant is a sacred agreement. God's sign joins a promise with duties toward life.

contextNote.title: Shared worth sets a limit on killing
contextNote.text: The account grounds its warning against bloodshed in God's image. This recalls the shared human identity stated at creation. The covenant also includes creatures that cannot make promises themselves. Its reach exceeds Noah's household even as the following family scene introduces division.

passages.title: Families and nations
passages.summary: The chapter lists peoples descended from Noah's sons.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: The family record joins many peoples to common ancestors. Consider the duties that shared humanity creates.

contextNote.title: Family language places nations within one world
contextNote.text: The list groups peoples by families, languages, lands, and nations. Differences remain visible within a common descent from Noah. Israel's later neighbors therefore enter the story before Israel itself. The family structure invites readers to see relationships across political boundaries.

passages.title: Babel and Terah's family
passages.summary: People build Babel. God confuses their speech. Terah's family travels from Ur toward Canaan.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: The Church manual contrasts Babel with the covenant family story. Consider how pride differs from trust.

contextNote.title: A great name competes with spreading across the earth
contextNote.text: The builders want a lasting name and protection against scattering. Their shared speech makes that plan possible. The scattering answers their stated aim rather than simply destroying a building. Abram's story next begins with departure and a promised name he cannot secure himself.

passages.title: Abram's call
passages.summary: Abram travels from Haran to Canaan. Famine leads him into Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham 2 links the covenant with blessing all families. Study the promise as a duty to serve.

contextNote.title: A promise reaches beyond the chosen household
contextNote.text: Abram receives a blessing whose stated reach includes other families. That outward purpose matters when famine takes him into Egypt. His attempt to protect himself then places Sarai and Pharaoh's household at risk. The chapter sets promised blessing beside conduct that brings trouble to others.

passages.title: Abram and Lot separate
passages.summary: Abram lets Lot choose land. Lot settles near Sodom. God renews Abram's promise.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham gives Lot the first choice. Consider how covenant living can support peace over advantage.

contextNote.title: Giving the first choice limits a family conflict
contextNote.text: The dispute begins with livestock and insufficient space for both households. Abram gives Lot the first choice rather than enforcing his senior position. Lot judges the land by its visible water supply. The account also names Sodom's wrongdoing, which the attractive landscape does not reveal.

passages.title: Lot rescued
passages.summary: Abram rescues Lot after a battle. Melchizedek blesses Abram.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Alma 13 expands Melchizedek's role as a priest. Keep that teaching distinct from Genesis's brief account.

contextNote.title: Rescue need not create dependence on a ruler
contextNote.text: Abram separates the rescue of Lot from accepting the king's wealth. His refusal prevents the king from claiming credit for Abram's prosperity. Yet he preserves the shares owed to his allies. Personal restraint does not cancel the claims of others who joined the work.

passages.title: God's covenant with Abram
passages.summary: God promises descendants to Abram. A covenant ceremony follows.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: God's promise meets Abraham's fear about an heir. Consider how faith can coexist with unanswered questions.

contextNote.title: The land promise includes a delay marked by suffering
contextNote.text: Abram asks about an heir and assurance concerning the land. The response includes generations of oppression before return. Promise and possession therefore do not occur within the same lifetime. The ceremony places Abram's immediate uncertainty inside a much longer family future.

passages.title: Hagar and Ishmael
passages.summary: Hagar flees harsh treatment from Sarai. God's messenger meets her. Ishmael is born.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: God sees Hagar in distress. Consider whose need you can recognize within unequal relationships.

contextNote.title: Seeing Hagar does not erase her unequal position
contextNote.text: Hagar speaks directly with God's messenger outside the household that harmed her. That encounter gives the enslaved woman a voice and a promise. The command to return nevertheless leaves a difficult tension in the account. Divine attention does not mean Sarai's harsh treatment becomes acceptable.

passages.title: New names and covenant
passages.summary: God names Abraham and Sarah. Circumcision becomes a covenant sign. God promises Isaac.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham 2 links covenant blessings with the gospel. Study both the promised blessing and its responsibility.

contextNote.title: The covenant sign includes people without equal household power
contextNote.text: Abraham applies the sign to sons and purchased servants alike. The household's shared duty reaches people with very different status. The promise concerning Isaac does not cancel the separate blessing of Ishmael. Read the covenant's common sign beside the account's unequal rights and different futures.

passages.title: Visitors and Abraham's plea
passages.summary: Visitors promise Sarah a son. Abraham pleads for Sodom.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham pleads for other people's lives. Consider how prayer can express care beyond your household.

contextNote.title: Abraham questions judgment through its effect on others
contextNote.text: Abraham asks whether innocent people will die with guilty people. His repeated questions reduce the number needed to spare the city. The exchange concerns collective punishment rather than only personal safety. A promised father of nations speaks about responsibility beyond his own household.

passages.title: Sodom and Lot's escape
passages.summary: Lot hosts visitors. A violent crowd threatens them. Lot's household escapes Sodom.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: How does Lot's family respond to the warning? What choices bring more harm afterward?

contextNote.title: Hospitality exposes a grave conflict over protection
contextNote.text: Lot tries to protect his guests by offering his daughters to the crowd. That choice endangers family members while claiming a duty toward visitors. The account's violence cannot be reduced to one breach of hospitality. Flight from the city also leaves the surviving family vulnerable and isolated.

passages.title: Abraham and Abimelech
passages.summary: Abraham calls Sarah his sister. God warns Abimelech in a dream.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Abraham's fear puts Sarah at risk. Consider the effects of choices made to protect yourself.

contextNote.title: Abraham's fear misjudges the people around him
contextNote.text: Abraham assumes that fear of God is absent in this place. Abimelech's protest and response complicate that assumption. The deception threatens a household that did not know Sarah's marriage. The outsider's conduct exposes a failure within the household carrying the promise.

passages.title: Isaac and Ishmael
passages.summary: Isaac is born. Hagar and Ishmael leave. God provides water. Abraham makes a treaty.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: God hears Hagar and Ishmael. How can we notice people who have been pushed away?

contextNote.title: Water answers exclusion with a means to survive
contextNote.text: The family celebration leads into the removal of Hagar and Ishmael. Their danger reveals a cost hidden behind the household's secure future. God's response supplies water and a future for the excluded son. The account preserves two promises without pretending the separation causes no suffering.

passages.title: The binding of Isaac
passages.summary: God tests Abraham. A messenger stops the sacrifice. A ram takes Isaac's place.
passages.uncertainty: Lines connect named places. They do not trace a surveyed ancient road.

lds.text: Jacob 4:5 links Abraham's offering with the Father's gift of Christ. Genesis itself stops Isaac's sacrifice.

contextNote.title: The reader knows something Isaac does not
contextNote.text: The opening calls the command a test before Isaac learns about the sacrifice. His question about the lamb increases the distance between their knowledge. Abraham's answer postpones the explanation rather than resolving his son's danger. The provided ram finally changes what the father's obedience requires him to do.

passages.title: Sarah's burial

guides.title: Genesis: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Creation gives people a shared worth
steps.text: The chapter gives people worth before it gives them work. Both women and men bear God’s image. No king receives that status alone. The command to rule follows this shared identity. Read dominion beside the blessing of life, not as permission for abuse.

steps.title: A grave becomes a claim to land
steps.text: Abraham has a promise of land but must buy a burial place. The account names the field, trees, witnesses, and payment. Those details make a public claim, not a private favor. Sarah’s grave ties the family’s future to a place. The promised land first becomes theirs through a death.

steps.title: Food storage creates political power
steps.text: Joseph’s dream reading becomes a plan for food storage. The plan needs officials, storehouses, and control of grain. That work changes who holds power during a famine. Chapter 47 later describes people giving property for food. Follow both rescue and dependence through this larger story.

textRoutes.title: Babel and Terah's family
textRoutes.summary: People build Babel. God confuses their speech. Terah's family travels from Ur toward Canaan.
textRoutes.detail: The builders want a lasting name and protection against scattering. Their shared speech makes that plan possible. The scattering answers their stated aim rather than simply destroying a building. Abram's story next begins with departure and a promised name he cannot secure himself.

textRoutes.title: Abram's call
textRoutes.summary: Abram travels from Haran to Canaan. Famine leads him into Egypt.
textRoutes.detail: Abram receives a blessing whose stated reach includes other families. That outward purpose matters when famine takes him into Egypt. His attempt to protect himself then places Sarai and Pharaoh's household at risk. The chapter sets promised blessing beside conduct that brings trouble to others.

textRoutes.title: Abram and Lot separate
textRoutes.summary: Abram lets Lot choose land. Lot settles near Sodom. God renews Abram's promise.
textRoutes.detail: The dispute begins with livestock and insufficient space for both households. Abram gives Lot the first choice rather than enforcing his senior position. Lot judges the land by its visible water supply. The account also names Sodom's wrongdoing, which the attractive landscape does not reveal.

textRoutes.title: Lot rescued
textRoutes.summary: Abram rescues Lot after a battle. Melchizedek blesses Abram.
textRoutes.detail: Abram separates the rescue of Lot from accepting the king's wealth. His refusal prevents the king from claiming credit for Abram's prosperity. Yet he preserves the shares owed to his allies. Personal restraint does not cancel the claims of others who joined the work.

textRoutes.title: Sodom and Lot's escape
textRoutes.summary: Lot hosts visitors. A violent crowd threatens them. Lot's household escapes Sodom.
textRoutes.detail: Lot tries to protect his guests by offering his daughters to the crowd. That choice endangers family members while claiming a duty toward visitors. The account's violence cannot be reduced to one breach of hospitality. Flight from the city also leaves the surviving family vulnerable and isolated.

textRoutes.title: The binding of Isaac
textRoutes.summary: God tests Abraham. A messenger stops the sacrifice. A ram takes Isaac's place.
textRoutes.detail: The opening calls the command a test before Isaac learns about the sacrifice. His question about the lamb increases the distance between their knowledge. Abraham's answer postpones the explanation rather than resolving his son's danger. The provided ram finally changes what the father's obedience requires him to do.

textRoutes.summary: Jacob leaves for Haran. At Bethel he dreams of a stairway reaching heaven.
textRoutes.detail: Jacob reaches Bethel while leaving a family conflict behind. He recognizes God's presence where he expected only a night's rest. The promised return answers his immediate loss of home. His vow also reveals that assurance and his own response develop during the journey.

textRoutes.title: Jacob leaves Laban
textRoutes.summary: Jacob's household leaves Haran. Laban pursues them. They make an agreement.
textRoutes.detail: Rachel and Leah describe their father as treating them like outsiders. Their words connect marriage payments with the loss of a family share. Jacob's complaint about wages is therefore not the household's only grievance. Departure answers several kinds of dependence, while the final agreement limits further interference.

textRoutes.title: Return to Bethel
textRoutes.summary: Jacob returns to Bethel. Rachel dies near Bethlehem. Isaac dies.
textRoutes.detail: Jacob asks the whole household to remove foreign gods before returning to Bethel. Worship therefore includes objects and loyalties carried through the journey. textRoutes.title: Burial and forgiveness
textRoutes.summary: Joseph buries Jacob in Canaan. He reassures his brothers. Joseph later dies in Egypt.
textRoutes.detail: The brothers fear that Jacob's death has removed their protection from Joseph. Their renewed request shows that an earlier welcome did not end their fear. Joseph refuses to claim God's place in judging them. His promise to feed their children turns reassurance into continuing material support.
